The order governed material turned over by prosecutors during discovery and restricted the defense’s ability to publicize that evidence. Prosecutors had sought limits to keep discovery within the defense process, while Trump objected that the proposed restrictions burdened his speech. staged_description.description_long: In August 2026, Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche raising concerns about Justice Department settlements they said rewarded President Trump’s political allies. The lawmakers alleged that the department was using the Treasury Department’s Judgment Fund to work around a now-defunct anti-weaponization fund. Their letter cited a $4.9 million settlement with the estate of Ashli Babbitt, who was killed during the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, and agreements involving former national security adviser Michael Flynn ($1.25 million), anti-abortion activist Mark Houck ($1 million) and former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page ($1.25 million). The settlements involved claims against the federal government; Democrats argued that paying them through the Judgment Fund continued the same political favoritism they had criticized in the earlier fund. Blanche had recently taken over as attorney general and was the recipient of the letter. The article reports lawmakers’ allegations and the amounts they cited, not a finding that the settlements were unlawful or that Blanche personally directed them. The dispute centered on how federal settlement payments were made and whether the administration had honored its stated end to the anti-weaponization fund.
